 Why some Americans are stockpiling for a 90-day power outage | CBC News Loaded World Why some Americans are stockpiling for a 90-day power outage
 The number of Americans stockpiling bottled water, non-perishable food and other emergency supplies has spiked over the past few weeks, a trend that has only accelerated in the wake of a series of high-profile tech outages. Doomsday prepping surged after misleading posts about Pentagon order. Then came the tech outages
 Mike Crawley · CBC News · Posted: Nov 20, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 9 hours ago Play Listen to this article Estimated 5 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. These shoppers at a Walmart in Florida were preparing for Hurricane Isaias to hit the U.S. coast of the Gulf of Mexico. In late October, the retailer saw a significant nationwide spike in purchases of emergency supplies, according to a spokesperson. (Marco Bello/Reuters) Social Sharing
 The number of Americans stockpiling bottled water, non-perishable food and other emergency supplies has spiked over the past few weeks, a trend that has only accelerated in the wake of a series of high-profile tech outages. 
 The jump in purchases has triggered questions to the highest levels of the administration, with both U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance trying to assure Americans there's no need for doomsday prepping. 
 "Tell them to relax, everything's good," Trump said in a Thursday interview with Fox News . "I'll let you know if there's a problem." 
 "A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,” Vance told Fox News earlier this week. “My answer to that is no."
 The evidence of stockpiling is far and wide, including U.S. media reports of recent spikes in sales of emergency supplies at stores in California, Ohio and Oklahoma . 
 Walmart customers were stocking up on more propane, bottled water and camping gear than usual earlier ​this month, a company spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday. 
 WATCH | Amid reports of panic buying, U.S. officials try to calm fears over tech outages: Trump officials grilled over tech outages that have Americans on edge
 November 18 | Duration closed caption 2:29 Top U.S. national security officials faced tough questions from lawmakers Thursday over a series of tech outages and disruptions affecting airports, banks and Microsoft services that have rattled the American public and raised concerns about panic buying. Survival Frog, an online U.S. retailer specializing in emergency supplies, says its sales volume shot up 450 per cent in the three weeks since Oct. 27, with new customers accounting for the bulk of the increase, Axios reported on Thursday.
 Since late October, Costco's U.S. sales data showed an increase in purchases of "rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, batteries and similar items seemingly in response to a variety of concerns on social media," a company executive told Bloomberg this week. 
 Stockpiling predates tech outages
 Web searches for "emergency supplies" are up 300 per cent in the past month compared with the same time period last year, according to Google Trends. 
 The start of the stockpiling began several weeks before the recent string of tech failures . 
 It traces back to misleading TikTok and Facebook posts that followed a directive from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. 
 Originally announced in late September, the Pentagon initiative dubbed FORTRESS America (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability) includes a plan for every major U.S. military installation to have the capability to generate its own electricity.
 The start of the stockpiling began several weeks before the recent string of tech failures. It traces back to misleading TikTok and Facebook posts that followed a directive from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters)
 "So bases remain lit, aircraft fly, and command centers stay online even if the civilian grid is taken down by cyberattack or sabotage," said the Pentagon news release on Hegseth's announcement. 
 On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details of Hegseth's directive, including a specific nugget about a 90-day time frame. 
 U.S. bases prep for 90 days without power
 "The Pentagon is preparing U.S. military bases to keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support as it prepares for the possibility of a major war that could cripple power grids, disrupt supply chains and threaten critical infrastructure on American soil," said the report. 
 Within days of that story, Google searches for "90 day power outage" spiked by 5,000 per cent and retailers saw jumps in customers buying emergency supplies. 
 Videos quickly mushroomed on TikTok and YouTube twisting the content of the Fox News story, either suggesting that the U.S. government was warning people to prepare for a 90-day blackout or that the government was itself preparing for a 90-day blackout. 
 By mid-November, multiple TikTok videos falsely claimed a 90-day power outage would hit the U.S. on Nov. 17, the fact-checking website PolitiFact reported .
 The government of Germany renewed its recommendation for stockpiling at least a three-day supply of such basics as bottled water and non-perishable ready-to-eat food. The photo shows items in an emergency kit from German humanitarian aid organization Malteser Hilfsdienst. (Thilo Schmuelgen/Reuters)
 Some events that actually happened likely did little to the quell the paranoia. 
 A cyberattack raised temperatures in hundreds of supermarket freezers across France in mid-October, spoiling tens of millions of euros worth of food. French authorities blamed Iran-backed hackers . 
 The U.K. government launched an official "Be Ready" campaign in October, urging the British people to prepare to be self-sufficient for 72 hours in the event of an emergency. 
 Then just two weeks later, the European Commission unveiled new emergency preparedness guidelines .
 Multiple tech outages have Americans asking: Can somebody fix this?
 As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
 And then came the cascade of outages that shut down Microsoft services, stranded hundreds of thousands of U.S. air passengers, blocked customers at some U.S. banks from doing transactions online and put the National Security Agency's classified communications network offline all in the space of six days . 
 Mehdi Hossain, an associate professor of marketing at the University of Rhode Island, has researched the panic buying that defined the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. 
 Luggage at San Diego International Airport, three days after the ground-stop order that led to the cancellation of some 20,000 flights across the U.S. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)
 Hossain says uncertainty over how the pandemic would unfold meant that people had no reference point for how they should prepare, while the high levels of anxiety over the potential seriousness of the threat triggered stockpiling that at times became irrational. 
 "What was really happening under the hood is the thought that, 'OK, if I don't prepare for this reality, and I suffer and my family suffers because of my lack of preparedness, I am going to regret it,'" Hossain told CBC News. 
 Trump's team scrambles to calm U.S. fears over tech outages
 Flights, banks, emails: What we know about a U.S. wave of tech outages
 He says some similar psychology appears to have been at work in recent weeks, fuelled by those false reports on social media.
 "It's a snowball kind of effect," Hossain said. "That fake news, when it validates with your fear, you start trusting it more than probably you should, and you start acting on it."
 ABOUT THE AUTHOR
 Mike Crawley Correspondent

He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years.
